entities.summary:
Gil de Siloé, a preeminent Castilian sculptor of Flemish origin, established a foundational presence in the Kingdom of Castile during the late 15th and early 16th centuries. Active primarily in Burgos, his distinctive style fused the intricate naturalism of Northern European Gothic traditions with the burgeoning decorative richness of the Isabelline Gothic, making him a pivotal figure in the transition towards the Renaissance in Spain. His oeuvre, characterized by dynamic compositions, elaborate ornamentation, and profound emotionality, profoundly influenced the sculptural landscape of the Iberian Peninsula, particularly under the patronage of the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella.

Siloé's most significant commissions include the monumental altarpiece of the Cartuja de Miraflores, completed around 1499, which features the tombs of King John II of Castile and Isabella of Portugal, and the tomb of Prince Alfonso, their son. These works showcase his mastery in carving alabaster and wood, employing a flamboyant Gothic vocabulary replete with intricate tracery, heraldic motifs, and expressive figures. His collaboration with other prominent artists, such as the architect Juan de Colonia and his son Simón de Colonia, was instrumental in defining the visual culture of Burgos Cathedral and other major ecclesiastical sites, solidifying the Isabelline style as a distinct artistic expression.
